did.unittitle: Metropolitan Association New York Conference United Church of Christ records, 1850-2025
did.abstract: The Metropolitan Association of the New York Conference of the United Church of Christ formed from the renaming of the New York City Congregational Church Association in 1963. The latter formed from the merger of the Congregational Church Extension Society of New York City and Brooklyn, which began 1892 to support and establish NYC churches, and the New York City Congregational Church Association, which succeeded the Manhattan-Brooklyn Conference in 1910. The Metropolitan Association and its predecessors aided their member churches and clergy by providing advice, financial assistance, licensure, building ownership, and other support as needed by the very diverse congregations and communities in NYC. This collection includes records related to or created by the Metropolitan Association and its predecessors with the majority concerning the member churches of the association. The records include correspondence, financial records, legal records, property records, reports, photographs, directories, histories, constitutions, and other documents from or for the association.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: The Metropolitan Association of the New York Conference of the United Church of Christ was formed from a series of mergers and name changes of congregational associations in New York City with the current association beginning in 1963. In 1841, the Manhattan Congregational Association was formed, and meetings were held until 1846 when they decided to form a new association. In 1847, the Manhattan Association was dissolved, and the Congregational Association of New York and Brooklyn was formed with the latter eventually changing its name to the New York and Brooklyn Association of Congregational Churches. The New York and Brooklyn Association merged with the Manhattan Conference in 1895 to become the Manhattan-Brooklyn Conference which was succeeded by the New York City Congregational Church Association in 1910. The New York City Congregational Church Association was then incorporated January 16, 1922, before it consolidated with the Congregational Church Extension Society of New York City and Brooklyn on April 15, 1924 as the New York City Congregational Church Association. The Congregational Church Extension Society of New York City and Brooklyn began October 1892 to support and establish churches in New York and Brooklyn and the surrounding areas before it merged with the New York City Congregational Church Association. On November 26th, 1963, the New York City Congregational Church Association renamed itself as the Metropolitan Association of the New York Conference of the United Church of Christ.

Throughout its history, the Metropolitan Association and its predecessors supported and advised New York City's churches, licensed and supported congregational ministers, provided financial assistance, and attended significant church events. The association also owned various properties when churches were unable to do so themselves along with the Deer Hill Conference Center which was used for church and ministerial retreats. Many of the church properties were sold either to the church when possible or on the market when the conference could no longer sustain them, with the Deer Hill property being sold in 1989. Due to the historical role and population makeup of New York City, the association and its member churches witnessed and were involved in various social movements and significant events, and they ministered to and dealt with very ethnically and racially diverse congregations and communities. Unfortunately, as church memberships and finances changed or declined over time, many churches closed or merged with other congregations while others joined other denominations or unaffiliated themselves from the Metropolitan Association for various reasons, but there were also new churches formed and affiliated with the association as it entered the twenty-first century.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains records relating to and created by the Metropolitan Association of the New York Conference of the United Church of Christ and its predecessor associations with the majority of the records related to the member churches of the association. The records include communications with or about the member churches or personnel connected to the churches and association, legal concerns and documents involving the association or the member churches, materials from the administration of the association, and other records sent to or created by the association. The collection includes correspondence, reports, histories, legal documents, financial statements, photographs, directories, minutes, constitutions, by-laws, aid applications, mortgages, building plans, and other documents.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The collection is arranged into two series with one series for association specific records and one for records relating to the churches within the association. The church records series is further arranged into seven subseries based on the regions or counties within the Metropolitan Association. Series 1: Association records is arranged chronologically by start date while Series 2: Church records is arranged alphabetically.

relatedmaterial.head: Related Materials
relatedmaterial.p: Additional records may be held by individual church archives such as those at Plymouth Church and the Riverside Church Archives. Records relating to the East Harlem Protestant Parish and the churches involved can be found in the East Harlem Protestant Parish records, 1942 -- 2007 collection at the Burke Library at Union Theological Seminary, Columbia University in the City of New York.

odd.head: Content Warning
odd.p: This collection includes content and language that may be upsetting or triggering. These records reflect the language and attitudes of the historical period in which they were created; many of these terms are unacceptable today. The Congregational Library & Archives works to preserve Congregational history and stories while acknowledging that sometimes that history is problematic or questionable. We do this to preserve, contextualize, and reflect on the past so that we may learn from it.
